alignment.note: Greek opens with the coordinating conjunction καί ('and'), the typical Markan paratactic chain. The Vulgate replaces this with the ablative-absolute relative pronoun Quo ('which thing'), folding the conjunction into the participial clause, while the Peshitta marks the transition with the postpositive ܕܝܢ in a later position.
γνοὺς (aorist participle of γινώσκω) / ܝܕܥ / cognito — all render 'having known/perceived', though Greek and Latin use a participle whereas Syriac uses a finite-style verb in narrative sequence.

The articular subject ὁ Ἰησοῦς stands after the participle in Greek; the Vulgate Jesus is postponed to follow ait illis; the Peshitta fronts ܝܫܘܥ to clause-initial position and inserts the discourse particle ܕܝܢ. These are stylistic word-order variants without semantic effect.
Greek λέγει is a vivid historic present ('he says'); the Vulgate ait and Syriac ܘܐܡܪ both render with past/perfective narrative aspect ('he said'), a routine tense-levelling in the versions.
αὐτοῖς / ܠܗܘܢ / illis — dative/lamadh of indirect object, 'to them'.
τί / ܡܢܐ / Quid — interrogative 'why/what'.

Greek διαλογίζεσθε is a single finite verb ('you reason/discuss'); the Peshitta uses the participle ܪܢܝܢ plus enclitic pronoun ܐܢܬܘܢ, the standard Syriac periphrastic present construction. The Vulgate cogitatis ('you think') narrows the sense of inner reasoning.
ὅτι / ܕ (prefixed to ܠܚܡܐ) / quia — causal conjunction 'because/that'.
Greek ἄρτους is plural ('loaves'); the Vulgate panes likewise plural; the Syriac ܠܚܡܐ is a collective/mass noun ('bread'), a normal idiomatic levelling of the count-plural into a collective.
Negation οὐκ / Latin non. The Syriac expresses the negated possession with the existential negator ܠܝܬ ('there is not').

Greek and Latin use the verb 'to have' (ἔχετε / habetis) with explicit subject 'you'; the Syriac employs the idiomatic existential-possessive construction ܠܝܬ ܠܟܘܢ ('there is not to you'), Semitic possession lacking a 'have' verb.

Greek οὔπω is a single negative-temporal adverb ('not yet'); the Vulgate nondum matches it; the Syriac analyses it into ܠܐ ܥܕܡܐ ܠܗܫܐ ('not until now'), an expanded periphrasis of the same temporal negation.

Greek νοεῖτε and Latin cognoscetis ('do you perceive/know') are finite; the Syriac uses the periphrastic participle ܝܕܥܝܢ + enclitic ܐܢܬܘܢ. Note the Vulgate's future cognoscetis where Greek has present, a minor tense divergence.
οὐδέ / ܘܠܐ / nec — coordinating negation 'nor'.

Greek συνίετε ('do you understand') and Latin intelligitis are finite; the Syriac again renders periphrastically with ܡܣܬܟܠܝܢ + enclitic ܐܢܬܘܢ, consistent with its handling of the parallel verbs of perception in this verse.
ἔτι / ܥܕܟܝܠ / adhuc — adverb 'still/yet'.

Greek πεπωρωμένην (perfect passive participle of πωρόω, 'made hard/calloused') describes a settled state of hardening. The Vulgate cæcatum ('blinded') shifts the metaphor toward blindness rather than callousness; the Syriac ܩܫܝܐ ('hard') retains the literal sense of hardness, matching the Greek root-image.

Greek ἔχετε and Latin habetis use the verb 'have' with the heart as object ('do you have a hardened heart'); the Syriac reverts to the existential-possessive idiom ܐܝܬ ܠܟܘܢ ('there is to you'), avoiding a 'have' verb in keeping with Semitic syntax.
Articular τὴν καρδίαν / ܠܒܐ / cor — 'the heart'; Syriac and Latin omit a separate article, the Syriac noun carrying the emphatic state.

Greek ὑμῶν and Latin vestrum supply an explicit possessive 'your' modifying 'heart'; the Syriac leaves the heart unmodified, the possession being already implied by the surrounding ܠܟܘܢ construction, so no separate pronoun is attested.
